title: GPU pulse profiling — short-burst resonance investigation
content:
Summary:

This doc captures an exploratory profiling session focused on repeated short bursts of decoder work that produce a recurring ‘pulse’ in GPU telemetry (utilization spikes followed by occupancy drops). The pattern shows up on some workloads served by the microbatching pipeline where token generation is bursty (user-driven chat + long context). We ran Nsight captures and CUDA-graph-enabled traces to understand SM wakeup/resonance, prefetch echoes, and kernel-handoff jitter.

Goals / questions:
- Reproduce the short-burst utilization pattern reliably in a controlled test.
- Determine whether the occupancy dips are due to KV cache prefetching, cudaGraph replay fragmentation, SM wake latency, or host-side scheduling jitter.
- Identify mitigations with minimal throughput/latency regressions (batch aperture tuning, prefetch coalescing, lightweight kernel padding).

Experimental setup:
- Cluster: dedicated-capacity p4d-like nodes (8x A100-40GB equivalent in our lab), driver 525.xx, CUDA 12.1, Nsight Systems 2024.3.
- Binary: serving-runtime main@commit f3a2b9c (microbatch pipeline, cudaGraph capture enabled).
- Workload: chat-style synthetic that alternates short user prompts (1–5 tokens) and long context decoding bursts (200–400 tokens) to force microbursting on the decoder.
- Capture: 3 Nsight traces (trace1/trace2/trace3) with 1s sampling + full timeline mode. Also collected per-SM perf counters (active_warps, issued_instructions, l2_hit_rate) and kernel name aliased by function id.

Key observations:
1) Repeating pulse shape in timeline: utilization rapidly rises to ~95% for 60–120 ms, then decays to 30–40% for ~80–150 ms, before the next burst. The tail-down correlates with a cluster of small memcpy async copies and short 'kv-prefetch' kernels.

2) Prefetch echo and occupancy shadowing: KV-prefetch kernels often run immediately after the main decoder kernel but at much lower parallelism (grid dims collapsed). They appear to evict active warps from L2/KV working set, causing a few subsequent decoder warps to stall due to memory miss churn. L2 miss counters spike ~8–12 ms after the prefetch kernel starts.

3) cudaGraph replay fragmentation: When replaying captured graphs with slightly different microbatching (timing jitter from host), the graph decomposes into two small exec fragments separated by a tiny host sync. This yields idle pockets where scheduled SMs go into a low-power standby and then pay a wakeup cost when next kernel arrives. The Nsight timeline shows tiny quiet periods (100–300 us) before the next decoder kernel during some replays.

4) SM wakeup / clock slack: On power/clock telemetry, SM clocks dip during quiet pocket and require ~200–400 us to ramp back under current p-state governor settings. For short bursts this ramp is not amortized.

5) Host-side scheduling jitter: The host thread responsible for CUDA graph launch occasionally experiences 50–200 us jitter due to lock contention in the batching queue when concurrency is high. Those jitter events align with the quiet pockets in ~35% of traces.

Microbenchmarks & repro notes:
- Synthetic microburst harness attached (see linked_artifacts) reproduces the pulse at ~95% fidelity. Tune knobs used: microbatch_size=1, max_batch_delay_ms=2, kv_prefetch=true/false toggle.
- When kv_prefetch is disabled, occupancy drop depth reduces by ~12–15% but raw latency increases 6–8% for the first token in a long decode.
- Forcing a tiny no-op kernel (single-block sleep kernel) immediately after cudaGraph replay prevents SM clock-down and eliminates the quiet pocket in 78% of cases; tail latency improves but end-to-end token cost slightly increases due to extra kernel.

Potential root causes (ranked):
1) Combined effect of small KV-prefetch kernels + cudaGraph fragmentation causing working-set churn and SM idle pockets.
2) SM clock governor reacting to brief idle periods.
3) Host-side batching lock contention occasionally amplifies the timing jitter.

Mitigation ideas to try (ordered by implementation complexity):
- Kernel coalescing: collapse KV-prefetch into the decoder kernel when possible (data-dependent). Reduces kernel count and prevents handoff churn. (Owner: Marcus).
- Lightweight filler kernel: insert an extremely cheap persistent-kernel or empty-block sleep of 64–128 us after replay to avoid clock ramp. Needs cost/throughput tradeoff analysis. (Owner: Elena).
- Prefetch throttling/coalescing: batch multiple prefetches into fewer larger prefetch kernels triggered on decode horizon. (Owner: Priya).
- Host-side scheduling fixes: reduce lock contention in batch queue (lock-free ring or finer-grained locking) to reduce 50–200 us jitter events. (Owner: Ravi).
- Adjust GPU clock/power policy for dedicated nodes for shorter ramp windows (ops/security permitting) — ops-aware.

Immediate next steps (short runway):
1) Marcus: prototype KV-prefetch-inlined decoder locally, measure tail and per-token throughput (due 2025-11-27).
2) Elena: implement filler kernel experiment in a canary release and run cluster A/B for 24 hours to measure token cost vs tail improvement (due 2025-11-25).
3) Ravi: add telemetry hooks to batch queue to capture contention stacks + histogram of scheduling jitter in production sampling (patch + feature flag, due 2025-11-22).
4) Priya: run a batch of cudaGraph replay permutations to quantify fragmentation sensitivity (submit matrix results to linked confluence page, due 2025-11-26).

Notes & open questions:
- Need to quantify customer-visible impact: how often do real chat workloads hit this microburst shape vs synthetic? Suggest sampling 1% of requests with nsight-lite traces for 48 hours behind feature flag.
- Evaluate cost of filler kernel at scale; we need to model per-token added GPU-seconds vs SLA tail reduction.
- Determine if a small change in microbatch batching policy (increase delay from 2ms -> 4ms) dramatically reduces pulses without hurting interactive latency.

Appendix: quick Nsight capture commands used
- nsight-sys profile: nsys profile --output=trace1 --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi --sample=1 --trace=cuda,nvtx --device-metrics-board
- nvprof-like perf counter dump attached via ncu: ncu --target-processes=all --metrics active_warps,sm_efficiency,l2_hit_rate -o ncu-report

Raw trace locations and references listed in linked_artifacts.

If you have other experiment ideas (e.g., persistent-kernel warmers, dynamic prefetch window), add them below or ping #serving-runtime with experimental tags.
